newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexicans protest U.S. execution of countryman.
newsitem.headline: Mexicans protest U.S. execution of countryman.

text.p: Mexicans waving banners angrily denouncing the scheduled U.S. execution of a Mexican fisherman on Wednesday gathered on a bridge on the Texan border clamouring for their countryman's life.

Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria sent a letter early on Wednesday to Texas Gov. George Bush, urging him to stay the execution of Irineo Tristan Montoya on humanitarian grounds for 30 days, while a final investigation into the case is carried out.
And the condemned man's father, Honourio Tristan, appealed to Mexican President Ernesto Zedillo in a live interview on TV Azteca to step in and persuade Bush to stay the execution.
The execution, scheduled for 6 p.m. CDT (2300 GMT) in Hunstville, Texas, has caused an uproar in Mexico, where the death penalty is banned and considered cruel and inhuman.

As Mexicans protested on a bridge between Matamoros, Mexico and Brownsville, Texas, and launched appeals in a last-ditch bid to save his life, Tristan bid farewell to his parents at the Texas jail where he is scheduled to die.

Tristan, convicted of stabbing to death a motorist in 1985, remained calm during the farewell visit by his parents and said he would remain that way to the end, Mexico's consul-general in Houston, Manuel Perez Cardenas, who witnessed the visit, told Televisa's midday news.
"He didn't shed a tear. He hasn't lost his strength, his emotional equilibrium, for a single moment and his optimism is still alive," he said.
The scheduled execution has sent shudders through the national psyche, particularly as many Mexicans feel the U.S. justice system is biased against their emigrees to the United States.
Tristan's lawyers say he signed a confession admitting to the murder without understanding a word of it, because he did not speak English. He has since said he is innocent.
Mexican authorities also allege international consular conventions were broken because Tristan was not informed of his right to contact a Mexican consul when he was arrested.

The U.S. Supreme Court was considering an 11th-hour appeal against the death sentence, which Mexican state news agency Notimex said would be just the fourth execution of a Mexican in the United States in 50 years.

In Mexico, television reports were topped by images of the 30-year-old Tristan behind bars, with cameras panning to the white gurney to which he will be strapped and injected with a concoction of lethal chemicals.
The afternoon paper La Prensa, sold on Mexico City streets, yelled in a banner headline "Today, they kill him."

Televisa TV network, which has repeatedly referred to the death penalty in this case as "administrative assassination", dwelt on the fact that the condemned man was denied his last wish of hugging his mother.
She is dying of lung cancer, and Mexico's consul-general said she had left hospital for two days to be with her son in the Huntsville jail.
